findings.diagnosis: The prompt underestimates the harm of cutting inside numeric expressions (numbers, ranges, units, percentages); splitting a numeral from its unit or the endpoints of a range produces incoherent or mistranslated numeric phrases when pieces are translated separately.
findings.evidence: en_us_419,en_us_1050,en_us_1116,en_us_950 — these cases all show cuts that split numbers/ranges or number+unit ("340 million to 500 million", "83 meters", "Nearly 200 ..." , "200 ... lives") and the target keeps the numeric phrase intact.

edit.text: Do not cut inside numeric expressions or ranges (numbers, multipliers like "million", units, percents, or the endpoints of a range); keep the whole numeric phrase together.

findings.diagnosis: The prompt undervalues keeping verbs with their core complements: it often allows cuts that strand verbs, prepositional objects, or infinitival complements, which produces orphaned predicates or reversed attachments in the joined translation.
findings.evidence: en_us_950,en_us_1600,en_us_167,en_us_390 — all show harmful splits that separate a verb or auxiliary from its object/complement or strand a prepositional/infinitival phrase (e.g. "trying to make" vs "contact with sailors", verb + object splits), and the target preserves predicate+arguments.

edit.text: Avoid cutting between a verb (or auxiliary) and its core object/complement or between a verb and its following prepositional/infinitival complement; keep predicate + core arguments together.

findings.diagnosis: The prompt does not sufficiently penalize cuts that create very short trailing fragments (one- or two-word pieces); such tiny fragments are frequent sources of contradiction or loss when translated separately in short-latency bins.
findings.evidence: en_us_1116,en_us_419,en_us_538,en_us_1050 — these examples show the policy leaving single-word or very-short trailing pieces (e.g. lone "said", isolated numerals, lone determiners/auxiliaries) while the target moves boundaries to avoid those tiny fragments.

edit.text: Prefer not to create trailing pieces of only one or two words (single-word predicates, lone determiners/nouns); avoid such tiny fragments unless preventing them would force a worse break of predicate or noun structure nearby.
